Most image dehazing algorithms in practical applications suffer from weak input adaptability due to their neglect of input image types (hazy or haze-free), and they often enhance dehazing performance by deepening network layers, resulting in large parameter counts that make real-time processing difficult. To address these issues, we propose a real-time image dehazing algorithm based on adaptive routing. Firstly, we design an adaptive routing module based on multi-scale feature extraction to determine the processing path of the input image. Then, based on the traditional feature attention (FA) module, a lightweight de-redundant feature attention (DRFA) module is constructed for dehazing processing. Finally, the residual network with the PixelShuffle upsampling module is utilized for efficient image recovery. The experimental results demonstrate that our algorithm achieves high PSNR and SSIM scores on several datasets, and we reach an average PSNR and SSIM of 26.75 dB and 0.832 on the mixed dataset of clear and hazy images, respectively. These results outperform other comparative algorithms, indicating the robustness and practicality of our approach. Not only that, our algorithm has a computational cost of 8.93G FLOPs and a dehazing time of only 4.81 ms during the 256 × 256-pixel image dehazing efficiency test, which meets the requirements of real-time processing for video surveillance in outdoor scenes. In hazy weather, light scattering caused by tiny particles degrades image quality, affecting clarity and visual perception, which can interfere with the performance of subsequent computer vision tasks, making image dehazing techniques crucial [ 1 – 3 ]. The traditional image dehazing algorithms mainly include image enhancement-based dehazing algorithms and prior-based dehazing algorithms. Among them, image enhancement-based dehazing algorithms can lead to color distortion and missing information in dehazed images because they do not consider the imaging mechanism of hazy weather. The prior-based dehazing algorithms usually use the atmospheric scattering model (ASM) [ 4 ] as their theoretical basis and combine it with handcraft priors to remove haze from the image. Such algorithms have achieved remarkable results in image dehazing, but they are overly dependent on specific scenes and prior assumptions, which leads to the limitation of their generalization ability and robustness. In recent years, with the rapid development of deep learning, deep learning-based dehazing algorithms have become the mainstream in this field. These algorithms use convolutional neural networks (CNN) to construct the dehazing network and achieve ideal dehazing results. Despite the significant advantages of such hazing algorithms, they still face the problems of weak model input adaptation and high computational cost in outdoor scenes. To address the problems above, we propose a real-time image dehazing algorithm based on adaptive routing, with the following contributions: • Aiming at the problems of poor robustness and adaptability of current dehazing algorithms in outdoor scenes, an adaptive routing module based on multiscale feature extraction is constructed. The module analyzes the multi-scale downsampled feature maps and scores the features of the input images in combination with the adaptive routing mechanism to decide whether the input images need to be dehazed, to improve the robustness and adaptability of the dehazing algorithm in outdoor scenes while saving unnecessary computational costs. • We design a lightweight de-redundant feature attention (DRFA) dehazing module to improve the dehazing algorithm’s efficiency by eliminating redundant information in low-resolution features. The module is based on the traditional feature attention (FA) module and introduces spatial and channel squeeze convolution (SCConv) to reduce feature spatial and channel redundancy. At the same time, the module uses residual concatenation to preserve the key feature information during the dehazing process. • To reduce the artifacts and checkerboard effects that occur during the upsampling process and

At the same time, the module uses residual concatenation to preserve the key feature information during the dehazing process. • To reduce the artifacts and checkerboard effects that occur during the upsampling process and improve the dehazing visual quality of our algorithm. We propose an upsampling module that combines a residual network and PixelShuffle. This module uses PixelShuffle to increase the image resolution and employs a convolutional layer to learn mapping and reconstruction information, achieving a high-quality output of reconstructed images with a relatively low number of parameters and computational cost. Early image dehazing techniques mainly rely on image enhancement algorithms to improve the contrast and clarity of images, thereby enhancing the visual quality of images. Commonly used algorithms include those based on histogram equalization, Retinex theory, and homomorphic filtering. For example, Xu et al. [ 5 ] proposed a dehazing algorithm based on contrast-limited adaptive histogram equalization, which can suppress noise while enhancing image contrast and improving the dehazing effect. Jobson et al. [ 6 ] proposed the multi-scale Retinex with color restoration (MSRCR) algorithm. By defining a color restoration method to correct image defects, it can restore high-definition images in low-light environment. Yu et al. [ 7 ] proposed a dehazing algorithm based on homomorphic filtering, which can not only improve the degradation of images but also effectively enlarge image details and enhance image contrast. The above dehazing algorithms have the advantages of simplicity and efficiency. However, ignoring the degradation factors of images will lead to problems such as loss of local image information and unsatisfactory dehazing effects. To more accurately restore clear images, researchers base their methods on the atmospheric scattering model, using reasonable assumptions and prior knowledge to estimate and reconstruct dehazed images. For example, He et al. [ 8 ] proposed a dark channel prior (DCP) algorithm, which estimates the atmospheric light and scene transmission in an image to remove haze, achieving effective dehazing results to some extent. Zhu et al. [ 9 ] introduced a color attenuation prior (CAP)-based dehazing algorithm that estimates the distribution of color attenuation caused by haze in images and then corrects the color attenuation effect to restore the color. Berman et al. [ 10 ] presented a non-local prior-based dehazing algorithm that utilizes statistical texture information from natural images to analyze and estimate the transmission of an image, allowing for better adaptation to different scenes. Although prior-based dehazing algorithms have achieved certain results, they rely heavily on specific scenes and prior assumptions, leading to poor generalization and robustness.

With the continuous progress of deep learning technology, deep learning-based algorithms have emerged in recent years to solve the problem of image dehazing. Cai et al. [ 11 ] proposed a DehazeNet network, which can estimate the medium transmittance of an image and bring it into the physical imaging model to obtain the restored K. Meng et al. 1019 Page 4 of 18 image. The AOD-Net dehazing algorithm proposed by Li et al. [ 12 ] deforms the atmospheric scattering model, combines atmospheric light and transmittance into one variable, and then generates a dehazed image through a convolutional neural network. The above algorithms are all based on the atmospheric scattering model to perform dehazing processing on images, but still cause problems such as color distortion due to the limitations of the physical model. The direct end-to-end dehazing algorithm no longer relies on the physical model and restores the clear image by learning the mapping between hazy images and clear images. For example, Dong et al. [ 13 ] proposed a multi-scale boosted dehazing network with dense feature fusion network (MSBDN). By developing a simple and effective enhanced decoder, the clear image is gradually restored. Hong et al. [ 14 ] proposed a knowledge distilling dehazing network (KDDN), which extracts image dehazing through heterogeneous task simulation. Guo et al. [ 15 ] proposed the DeHamer dehazing network, which enhances the dehazing performance by learning a modulation matrix based on Transformer features to modulate CNN features and introducing a prior related to haze density. Although deep learning-based dehazing algorithms exhibit excellent performance in dehazing effects, they may still face issues such as input adaptability and find it difficult to meet the usage requirements of outdoor scenes. To further enhance the generalization and adaptability of dehazing network models, Wang et al. [ 16 ] proposed an end-to-end haze concentration adaptive network (HCAN). This network uses a pyramid feature extractor to obtain features of different layers and, through the feature enhancement module, adaptively perceives and integrates hazy images of different concentrations, ultimately restoring a clear image. Yu et al. [ 17 ] proposed an adaptive multi-information distillation dehazing network. Through a multi-information distillation module, it adaptively assigns weights to different haze regions and gradually extracts important features to restore different types of h

image. Yu et al. [ 17 ] proposed an adaptive multi-information distillation dehazing network. Through a multi-information distillation module, it adaptively assigns weights to different haze regions and gradually extracts important features to restore different types of hazy images. Li et al. [ 18 ] proposed an attention-based adaptive feature selection for multistage image dehazing network (ASNet). By adaptively selecting and aggregating, it extracts rich detailed features to restore hazy images with different concentrations and uneven distributions. Although these algorithms possess certain adaptive capabilities, they still suffer from issues such as over-processing for clear input images, and their high parameter count and latency significantly restrict their application in real-time scenarios.

The overall framework of the algorithm is shown in Fig. 1 . First, the features of the input image are scored through the adaptive routing module to determine whether the image needs to enter the dehazing process. The inputs judged as clear will be directly output, while the hazy will be directed to the dehazing processing branch. Subsequently, the hazy inputs will be processed by multiple cascaded lightweight dehazing modules. The processed dehazing features will be fused adaptively with A real‑time image dehazing algorithm based on adaptive routing﻿ Page 5 of 18 1019 Fig. 1 Overall framework for the proposed network the downsampled features before dehazing. Finally, the dehazing result will be reconstructed and generated through the upsampling module that combines the residual network and PixelShuffle.

In most existing dehazing algorithms, the necessity of choosing an appropriate processing branch according to different input image types is often overlooked, which may lead to problems of incomplete dehazing or excessive dehazing in practical application scenarios. In fact, there is usually an obvious pixel-level difference between clear images and haze images in specific areas, which is particularly significant in real hazy images. To utilize this characteristic, we design an adaptive routing module based on multi-scale feature extraction. This module can analyze downsampled feature maps of different scales, score the input image, and determine the subsequent processing strategy accordingly. Specifically, if the score of the image is lower than the set threshold, we will directly output it without performing dehazing processing; if the score is higher than the threshold, the image will enter the dehazing processing branch for corresponding clarification processing, and finally generate the dehazed image. This adaptive strategy not only better meets the needs of different weather scenarios to improve dehazing efficiency, but also ensures higherquality image reconstruction. First, the downsampled features at each scale are subjected to global average pooling to effectively extract the key information of the features at each scale, and these pooled features are concatenated together to form a comprehensive multi-scale spliced feature F all . After training the adaptive routing module, a soft threshold score can be obtained. By setting a continuous threshold parameter between 0 and 1, the adaptive routing module can precisely adjust the processing ratio of hazy and clear images. As the threshold decreases, the network will perform dehazing processing on more images. Conversely, increasing the threshold means that more images will be directly output.

Inspired by the efficient feature attention (FA) dehazing module proposed by FFANet [ 19 ], AECR-Net [ 20 ] proves that simple modules can also achieve efficient dehazing effects by only using a few cascaded FA blocks. However, diverse redundant information in low-resolution features may mislead the attention to key features during dehazing processing. Therefore, we propose a lightweight de-redundant feature attention (DRFA) dehazing module. This module can more effectively focus on key features during dehazing and reduce the interference caused by redundant information. The structure of the DRFA dehazing module is shown in Fig. 2 . To reduce the negative impact of redundant information on local feature attention and the additional computational overhead caused by redundant information, we optimize based on the original FA dehazing module and replace regular convolution with SCConv convolution that reduces spatial and channel redundancy. SCConv consists of two sequentially placed units, the spatial reconstruction unit (SRU) and the channel reconstruction unit (CRU), which can reduce information redundancy in Fig. 2 Structure of the de-redundant feature attention (DRFA) dehazing module A real‑time image dehazing algorithm based on adaptive routing﻿ Page 7 of 18 1019 both spatial and channel dimensions. It can both reduce the computational burden and facilitate the focus on key features, thus enhancing the model’s ability to capture details. While constructing the network, we reused the original input features several times and screened the complex features extracted by the attention mechanism through SCConv to remove the redundant information. Eventually, the unprocessed original input features are fused with the enhanced local features and output, which highlights the key local features in the feature map, and also retains the integrity of the original information, achieving significant suppression of haze and overall improvement of image quality.

During image reconstruction, the choice of different upsampling algorithms can lead to different forms of representation of deep features after dimension space expansion. For instance, although commonly used interpolation algorithms can rapidly expand the spatial size, they rely too much on local pixel features and are not as effective in reconstructing image details. On the other hand, the more commonly used transposed convolution algorithm can achieve better reconstruction results through parameter learning; however, it is sensitive to hyperparameters such as convolution kernel size and step size, which is prone to the checkerboard effect in the generated image. To address the above problems, in the upsampling reconstruction stage, we propose an upsampling module that combines the convolution of residual structures with PixelShuffle to replace the commonly used transposed convolution for image restoration. This module can train the recovery of upsampled features at a lower cost of number of parameters and computational latency, and generates higher-quality dehazed reconstructed images. The proposed upsampling module first increases the number of channels of the low-resolution feature map by 1 × 1 convolution for subsequent channel transformation operations. Then image resolution enhancement is performed using PixelShuffle, and a convolutional layer is added to learn the mapping and reconstruction information. Unlike the traditional onetime upsampling operation that directly restores the input image size, we use multiple enlargements of the resolution of the deep features after dehazing until they are restored to the original size. This method can highlight the key feature information to avoid losing too much image information during the upsampling process of oversize transformation, which leads to degradation of the quality of the dehazed reconstructed image. We train and test on the RESIDE [ 21 ] dataset as well as NH-HAZE [ 22 ] and DenseHAZE [ 23 ] datasets. Among them, the RESIDE dataset is a large-scale synthetic dataset, and its subset contains hazy images and corresponding clear images in different indoor and outdoor environments. Since we mainly focus on outdoor scenes, the outdoor training set (OTS) subset is selected as the training set, and 36,000 hazy–clear image pairs are extracted as training samples. In the testing phase, the effectiveness and generalization of the model are evaluated using the subset synthetic objective testing set-outdoor (SOTS-Outdoor). Concurrently, to enhance the model’s capacity for dehazing in authentic scenarios, we have selected the real hazy datasets NH-HAZE and Dense-HAZE to augment the training dataset.

In order to deeply explore the influence of the upsampling algorithm on the effect of dehazing reconstructed images, we randomly selected 10 training images in the Dense-HAZE and NH-HAZE datasets and constructed a hybrid dataset for ablation experiments. In the experiments, we will use the model of conventional transposed convolution as the Baseline. Then, we replace the upsampling algorithm with the interpolation algorithm and the proposed upsampling algorithm with the residual structure in turn, respectively. The experimental results are shown in Table 7 . The results of ablation experiments show that the parameter learning-based upsampling algorithms (i.e., transposed convolution and the proposed upsampling algorithm) outperform the interpolated upsampling algorithms in the evaluation metrics of the dehazing results. In addition, the proposed upsampling algorithm, through the combination of residual structure and PixelShuffle, achieves a better dehazing reconstruction by improving the PSNR and SSIM by 0.47 dB and 0.06, respectively, compared to the method using transposed convolution.

Aiming at the problems of poor input adaptation and high computational cost faced in the process of dehazing in outdoor scenes, we propose a real-time image dehazing algorithm based on adaptive routing. Specifically, we first design an adaptive routing module based on multi-scale feature extraction, which analyzes the downsampled feature maps at different scales and scores the features of the input images by using the adaptive routing mechanism to determine whether they need to enter the dehazing process. For images judged as clear, the algorithm will output them directly, while hazy images will be guided to the dehazing processing branch. In addition, we propose a DRFA module. This module is optimized based on the traditional FA module and introduces the SCConv convolution to replace the regular convolution, aiming at reducing spatial and channel redundancy. Finally, we propose an upsampling module that combines residual networks and PixelShuffle to achieve effective recovery of upsampled features with low parametric and computational costs, while ensuring high-quality outputs of dehazed reconstructed images. The experimental results show that the proposed dehazing algorithm exhibits better dehazing performance on both synthetic hazy datasets and real hazy datasets, and improves the real-time performance of the algorithm without significantly reducing the dehazing effect. It also has a certain adaptive processing capability, which can better meet the needs of different scenarios. On SOTSOutdoor, we achieved high PSNR score (33.67dB) and SSIM score (0.984). On NH-HAZE, the highest PSNR score (21.70dB) and the third highest SSIM score (0.6952) were obtained, and the second highest PSNR (16.17dB) and the top SSIM score (0.4538) were achieved on Dense-HAZE, which were only 0.45dB lower than the top-ranked DeHamer, respectively, and 0.1064. In the case of clear image and haze image mixed input, we obtained the highest PSNR (26.75dB) and SSIM score (0.832), much higher than the scores of other comparison algorithms. The proposed algorithm shows significant advantages in terms of operation efficiency. During the inference efficiency test of 256 × 256-pixel images, our algorithm has a computational cost of 8.93G FLOPs, and the inference time consumed is only 4.81ms, which makes it very suitable for edge devices and tasks with high real-time requirements. Although our algorithm significantly reduces computational overhead, it inevitably compromises dehazing performance to some extent. Therefore, in future work, we plan to further improve the image restoration quality by designing more efficient dehazing modules.
